issues.issue: The Initial Period ends eight months after delivery of the Master Recordings comprising the "Recording Obligation", a term the agreement never defines (paragraph 2.02 defines only "Minimum Recording Obligation"). The end date of the Term therefore turns on an undefined phrase.

The warranty that Artist will record "exclusively for Grantor and PRI" sits awkwardly with PRI's engagement of Grantor to furnish "exclusive services", leaving the scope of the exclusivity (and to whom it runs) open.

"To the best of their ability" and "first-class standards for production in the Phonograph Record industry" are undefined performance benchmarks with no measurable content. A court would have to supply the standard.

PRI may disapprove a Composition for defamation, libel or infringement "or which is subject to Objection for any other legal reason whatsoever", and may disapprove a studio if its use "would otherwise in any way substantially hinder or prevent" recording; these catch-alls sit against the enumerated specifics and their reach is uncertain.

Masters must be "technically satisfactory" and embody Recordings that are "first-class (as that term is understood in the record industry)"; whether a delivery qualifies is left to an undefined industry standard that both sides could read differently. This is the classic acceptance-standard ambiguity in recording agreements.

"Reasonably consistent in concept and style" and "similar in general artistic concept and style" set a purely subjective artistic benchmark with no ascertainable boundary. A dispute over whether a delivered Album complied would turn entirely on that phrase.

Delivery dates "may be reasonably extended" if the parties "mutually agree in writing, based on good business judgment" — an agreement-to-agree qualified by two undefined standards. Whether either party could refuse an extension is unresolved.

Paragraph 4.01(d)(i) says late delivery within sixty days is not a failure to comply or a breach, but paragraph 6.01(c) reduces the Advance by 10% per month from "the last date such Album would otherwise be timely delivered pursuant to paragraph 4.01". Whether the sixty-day grace shifts that Final Date cannot be resolved from the two provisions read together.

Saying the "delivery date ... shall be suspended until such time as the parties so agree" is imprecise — a date cannot be suspended, and the clause gives no outer limit or mechanism if the parties never agree on the co-producer. The effect on the Contract Period and the Term is left open.

"Satisfactory completion" of the Article 3 and 4 procedures is made the condition of delivery without saying whose satisfaction governs or by what standard. The final clause then deems accepted and released Masters to count, which cuts against the preceding non-waiver language.

The second sentence is syntactically muddled: "if the parties do not reach such agreement or if neither party gives notice ... as provided above earlier than thirty (30) days prior to the date of initial release" leaves it unclear whether the thirty-day qualifier attaches to the notice or to the deemed date. The deemed delivery date therefore cannot be computed with confidence.

Masters are declared "work made for hire" and, in the alternative, assigned; whether a recording by an independent Grantor can qualify as a work made for hire is a recurring point of construction. The belt-and-braces drafting invites a dispute over which characterisation controls.

The chapeau of 5.01(b) confines the sub-clauses to "sales of Records in the United States during the Term", yet paragraph 3.03 makes PRI's use of out-takes subject to 5.01(b)(i) generally, leaving the territorial and temporal reach of the out-take consent unclear.

"A label used by PRI ... for Recordings of PRI's top 'pop' artists then under exclusive term contract" is a vague and shifting description, and whether a heavy-metal artist's Album falls within a "pop" label commitment is contestable. The obligation cannot be applied without construing "top 'pop' artists".

"Premium use" is not defined anywhere in the provision, and paragraph 7.05(a) separately prices "premium Records" without defining them either. The scope of the consent right turns on an undefined term.

Grantor is given approval over the Artwork, yet "any matter other than the Album cover layout and the picture or art to be used on the cover" is left to PRI's sole discretion; the boundary between the approved "Artwork" and PRI's reserved matters is uncertain.

The provision first limits PRI's exemption to sales "occurring prior to PRI's receipt of such notice" and then, in the same sentence, states PRI "shall have no liability by reason of such sales at any time", which swallows the obligation entirely. The two limbs cannot both be given effect.

The chapeau of paragraph 5.01(b) confines its sub-clauses to "sales of Records in the United States during the Term", yet this sub-clause governs sales of Albums outside the United States. The two cannot be squared on their face.

Editing costs are said to be "at PRI's expense" and yet "shall constitute an Advance hereunder", i.e. recoupable from Grantor's royalties; those two characterisations point in opposite directions. Who ultimately bears the cost is genuinely open.

The clause excludes such costs from "the applicable Recording Fund provided for in paragraph 6.01", but paragraph 6.01 establishes Advances and contains no "Recording Fund". The cross-reference has no referent in the instrument.

Paragraph 5.01(d)(viii) gives PRI and its licensees "the continuing right at all times" to manufacture and sell recompilation Albums, expressly subject only to 5.01(b)(ix)(B), which appears to override the three-Album ceiling imposed by this provision. The two rights cannot readily be harmonised.

The provision gives Grantor "five (5) business days" to object but later refers to "said five (5) day period", so the length of the objection window is internally inconsistent. That mismatch changes whether an objection was timely.

The compact-disc release obligation applies only "if commercially possible", an undefined and highly elastic qualifier that could excuse performance almost entirely. Whether the obligation binds at all turns on that phrase.

All of Grantor's protections in 5.01(b) fall away if Grantor has not "Materially fulfilled" its Article 3 and 4 delivery obligations, a materiality standard nowhere defined. The trigger for losing a substantial package of rights is left to construction.

The release remedy is conditioned on Grantor having "fulfilled all of its material obligations hereunder", an undefined standard, and the cure/termination sequence uses overlapping thirty- and sixty-day periods whose starting points are hard to fix. Both sides could reasonably compute the deadlines differently.

The condition is that Grantor obtain "all consents required by PRI" and "all agreements which PRI may require", giving PRI an unbounded ability to defer the reassignment right conferred by 5.01(c). The limits of what PRI may "require" are undefined.

This tail-piece excludes November and December from the computation while the parallel tail-piece to paragraph 5.01(d) excludes October, November and December; the two adjacent suspension rules use different exclusions without explanation. A party could argue the discrepancy is a drafting slip.

The Release Territories include "Benelux" and "Scandinavia", neither of which is defined, while paragraph 7.03(c) instead names Sweden and Denmark individually; which countries trigger the release obligation is therefore uncertain. The scope of the obligation turns on those undefined regional labels.
